style: Comprehensive meaningful blend (interpretive text) + amplified study form; bare transliterations in amp with Strong's carried in notes; em-dashes used sparingly; transliterations ASCII-normalized relative to the lexicon's spellings. Ecclesiastes uses Elohim throughout — the divine name YHWH never appears in the book and is never inserted.
chapterNote: The second experiment: if wisdom could not balance the books, perhaps pleasure can. The king pours himself into laughter, wine, building projects, gardens, servants, silver, singers, everything the eyes could ask -- and he is careful to tell us his wisdom stayed at the helm the whole time, for this is research, not mere indulgence. The verdict comes back the same: vapor, nothing left over. Worse, death levels the wise man with the fool, and the estate he built goes to a successor who may squander it. Yet at the bottom of the despair the chapter turns on a hinge (vv. 24-26): the simple goods of eating, drinking, and finding satisfaction in one's work are real after all, not as achievements wrung from life but as gifts received from the hand of God.

1.text: I said in my heart, 'Come now, let me test you with gladness, so drink in pleasure and see what good is in it.' But look, this also proved to be vapor.
1.amp: I said [amar] in my heart [leb], 'Come now, I will test [nasah -- prove by trial] you with mirth [simchah -- gladness, celebration], therefore see [raah] what is pleasant [tov]': and behold, this also is vapor [hebel].
1.notes: nasah (H5254) is to put to the proof, the word used of testing metal or testing God; pleasure here is a controlled experiment, not a surrender. simchah (H8057) is festive gladness, and the result is the refrain hebel (H1892), vapor.

2.text: Of laughter I said, 'It is madness,' and of gladness, 'What does this actually accomplish?'
2.amp: I said [amar] of laughter [sechok], 'It is mad [halal -- raving, boasting emptily]': and of mirth [simchah], 'What does it do [asah]?'
2.notes: sechok (H7814) is laughter shading into derision, and halal (H1984), which elsewhere means to praise or shine, here carries its darker sense of raving. The question is the bookkeeper's again: what does gladness produce?

3.text: I searched out in my heart how to draw my flesh along with wine, my heart still steering me with wisdom, and how to take hold of folly, until I could see what is good for the sons of man to do under heaven through the numbered days of their lives.
3.amp: I sought [tur -- explored, spied out] in my heart [leb] to draw [mashak -- pull along] my flesh [basar] with wine [yayin], my heart still guiding [nahag -- driving, conducting] me with wisdom [chokmah]; and to lay hold [achaz -- grasp, seize] on folly [sikhluth], till I might see [raah] what was that good [tov] for the sons of men to do [asah] under heaven [shamayim] all the days [yom] of their life [chay].
3.notes: tur (H8446) again, the scout's word: even the wine is reconnaissance. mashak (H4900) is to draw or drag ('to draw my flesh with wine', so the KJV margin), nahag (H5090) is to drive as a charioteer drives, and achaz (H270) to grasp firmly; the king kept one hand on folly and the other on the reins.

4.text: I made my works great: I built myself houses, and I planted myself vineyards.
4.amp: I made me great [gadal] works [maaseh]; I built [banah] me houses [bayith]; I planted [nata] me vineyards [kerem]:
4.notes: gadal (H1431), to make great; banah (H1129), to build and establish; nata (H5193), to plant and fix in place. The 'me... myself' drumbeat of vv. 4-8 is the Hebrew's own: every project bends back toward the builder.

5.text: I made myself gardens and parks, and in them I planted trees bearing every kind of fruit.
5.amp: I made [asah] me gardens and orchards [parks, pleasure-grounds], and I planted [nata] trees [ets] in them of every kind of fruit:
5.notes: The word for 'orchards' (H6508) is pardes, a Persian loanword for a walled pleasure-park, the word that gives us 'paradise'; the king was rebuilding Eden by hand. nata (H5193), to plant, echoes God's own planting of the first garden (cf. Genesis 2:8).

6.text: I made myself pools of water, reservoirs to irrigate the young forest where the trees were growing.
6.amp: I made [asah] me pools [berekah -- reservoirs] of water [mayim], to water from them the wood that brings forth [tsamach -- sprouts, causes to grow] trees [ets]:
6.notes: berekah (H1295) is an engineered reservoir, and tsamach (H6779) is the verb of sprouting growth. The scale is royal waterworks: he did not merely keep a garden, he watered a forest.

7.text: I bought male and female servants, and had servants born in my house; I also had herds and flocks in great number, more than all who were in Jerusalem before me.
7.amp: I got [qanah -- acquired, bought] me servants [ebed] and maidens, and had servants born in my house [bayith]; also I had great [rabah] possessions [miqneh -- livestock, property] of herds [baqar] and flocks [tson] above all that were in Jerusalem before [panim] me:
7.notes: qanah (H7069) is to acquire or purchase, and miqneh (H4735) is wealth counted in livestock. 'Servants born in my house' is literally 'sons of my house' (the KJV margin): an estate so established it reproduced itself.

8.text: I gathered for myself silver and gold as well, the private treasure of kings and of the provinces; I got myself men singers and women singers, and the delights of the sons of man, a harem of many concubines.
8.amp: I gathered me also silver [keseph] and gold [zahab], and the peculiar treasure of kings and of the provinces [medinah]: I got me men singers and women singers [shir], and the delights of the sons of men, concubine upon concubine [shiddah], of every sort.
8.notes: shiddah (H7705), doubled in the Hebrew, is an obscure word the KJV took as 'musical instruments' but which most likely means women of the harem, captives or concubines; the list climaxes where a king's appetite does. keseph (H3701) and zahab (H2091) are the silver and gold of tribute, the 'peculiar treasure' of vassal kings and provinces.

9.text: So I became great, increasing beyond all who were before me in Jerusalem, and through it all my wisdom stood with me still.
9.amp: So I was great [gadal], and increased [yasaph] more than all that were before [panim] me in Jerusalem: also my wisdom [chokmah] remained [amad -- stood firm] with me.
9.notes: amad (H5975), to stand firm: the experimental control held. His chokmah (H2451) never left the room; whatever the verdict, it cannot be blamed on drunkenness.

10.text: Whatever my eyes asked for I did not withhold from them; I refused my heart no gladness, for my heart found joy in all my toil, and this joy was my portion, all my toil ever paid me.
10.amp: And whatever my eyes [ayin] desired [shaal -- asked, requested] I kept not [atsal] from them, I withheld [mana] not my heart [leb] from any joy [simchah]; for my heart rejoiced [sameach] in all my labour [amal]: and this was my portion [cheleq] of all my labour.
10.notes: shaal (H7592) is to ask, as of a petition granted; nothing the eyes petitioned for was denied. cheleq (H2506) is the allotted share, the inheritance-portion: of the whole vast estate, the only thing the labor actually paid out was the fleeting pleasure of the laboring itself.

11.text: Then I turned and faced all the works my hands had made, and the toil I had toiled to accomplish, and look: it was all vapor and a chasing after wind, and under the sun there was no profit at all.
11.amp: Then I looked [panah -- turned to face] on all the works [maaseh] that my hands had wrought [asah], and on the labour [amal] that I had laboured [amal] to do: and, behold, all was vapor [hebel] and a chasing after wind [reuth ruach], and there was no profit [yithron] under the sun [shemesh].
11.notes: panah (H6437) is to turn and face squarely: the honest audit. The verdict stacks all three thesis-words at once, hebel (H1892), reuth (H7469) with ruach (H7307), and no yithron (H3504), no surplus when the books were balanced.

12.text: Then I turned to consider wisdom, and madness, and folly side by side; for what can the man do who comes after the king? Only what has already been done.
12.amp: And I turned [panah] myself to behold [raah] wisdom [chokmah], and madness, and folly [sikhluth]: for what can the man [adam] do that comes [bo] after [achar] the king? even that which has been already [kebar] done [asah].
12.notes: The experiment was definitive because the experimenter was: no successor (achar, H310, the one coming after) will ever command more resources to re-run it. kebar (H3528), 'already', the Preacher's signature word again.

13.text: And I did see that wisdom has the advantage over folly, as real as the advantage of light over darkness.
13.amp: Then I saw [raah] that wisdom [chokmah] excels [yithron -- has the surplus, the advantage over] folly [sikhluth], as far as light [or] excels darkness [choshek].
13.notes: yithron (H3504), the profit-word, used twice here as 'excellency': within this life wisdom genuinely out-earns folly, as or (H216), light, out-serves choshek (H2822), darkness. The Preacher is no cynic about wisdom's relative worth.

14.text: The wise man has his eyes in his head where they belong, while the fool walks in darkness; and yet I came to know that one and the same event happens to them all.
14.amp: The wise man's [chakam] eyes [ayin] are in his head [rosh]; but the fool [kesil] walks [halak] in darkness [choshek]: and I myself perceived [yada] also that one [echad] event happens [qarah -- befalls, meets] to them all.
14.notes: kesil (H3684) is the thick, dull fool of Proverbs. qarah (H7136) is to befall or happen upon, and the 'one event' (echad, H259) is death itself: the great leveler that empties wisdom's advantage at the grave's edge.

15.text: So I said in my heart, 'What happens to the fool will happen to me also; why then have I been so exceedingly wise?' And I said in my heart that this too is vapor.
15.amp: Then said [amar] I in my heart [leb], 'As it happens to the fool [kesil], so it happens [qarah] even to me; and why was I then more [yother] wise [chakam]?' Then I said [dabar] in my heart, that this also is vapor [hebel].
15.notes: yother (H3148), the advantage or excess, kin to yithron: what is the surplus of my surplus wisdom? The Hebrew doubles the pronoun, 'it happens to me, even to me' (so the KJV margin), the king feeling death's aim settle on his own chest.

16.text: For the wise man is no more remembered than the fool forever, since in the days to come everything will already have been forgotten. And how does the wise man die? Just like the fool.
16.amp: For there is no remembrance [zikkaron] of the wise [chakam] more than of the fool [kesil] for ever [olam]; seeing that which now is, in the days [yom] to come [bo] shall all be forgotten [shakach]. And how dies the wise man? as the fool.
16.notes: shakach (H7911), to forget and neglect: the same forgetting that erased the generations in chapter 1 now erases the distinction wisdom bought. The dying question is nearly a cry: chakam (H2450) and kesil (H3684) share one grave.

17.text: So I hated life itself, because the work done under the sun lay heavy and grievous on me; for all of it is vapor and a chasing after wind.
17.amp: Therefore I hated [sane] life [chay]; because the work [maaseh] that is wrought [asah] under the sun [shemesh] is grievous [ra] unto me: for all is vapor [hebel] and a chasing after wind [reuth ruach].
17.notes: sane (H8130) is full-strength hatred, not mild distaste; the researcher's detachment has collapsed. ra (H7451), grievous, evil in its effect: the whole enterprise of life under the sun pressed on him like a wound.

18.text: And I hated all my toil, everything I had labored at under the sun, because I must leave it behind to the man who comes after me.
18.amp: Yea, I hated [sane] all my labour [amal] which I had laboured at [amel] under the sun: because I should leave [yanach -- set down, deposit] it unto the man [adam] that shall be after [achar] me.
18.notes: yanach (H3240) is to set something down and walk away: the estate is not taken, it is deposited with a stranger. The builder's grief is not that the work ends but that it changes hands.

19.text: And who knows whether that man will be wise or a fool? Yet he will be master over all my toil, everything my labor and my wisdom achieved under the sun. This also is vapor.
19.amp: And who knows [yada] whether he shall be a wise [chakam] man or a fool [sakal]? yet shall he have rule over all my labour [amal] wherein I have laboured [amal], and wherein I have shown myself wise [chakam] under the sun. This is also vapor [hebel].
19.notes: sakal (H5530), to play the fool: the heir is an unknown quantity holding a known fortune. History answered the question quickly, for Solomon's own heir Rehoboam split the kingdom within a year (cf. 1 Kings 12).

20.text: So I turned my heart around and gave it over to despair concerning all the toil I had toiled at under the sun.
20.amp: Therefore I went about [savav -- turned around] to cause my heart [leb] to despair [yaash -- give up hope] of all the labour [amal] which I took under the sun.
20.notes: yaash (H2976) is to abandon hope outright, despair as a settled act rather than a mood. savav (H5437), to turn about: the same circling motion as the wind of chapter 1, but now it is the man's own heart going around.

21.text: For here is a man whose toil was done with wisdom, with knowledge, and with real skill, and he must hand it all over as a portion to a man who never toiled for any of it. This also is vapor, and a great evil.
21.amp: For there is [yesh] a man [adam] whose labour [amal] is in wisdom [chokmah], and in knowledge [daat], and in equity [with skill and success]; yet to a man that has not laboured [amal] therein shall he give [natan] it for his portion [cheleq]. This also is vapor [hebel] and a great [rav] evil [ra].
21.notes: The word for 'equity' (H3788) is kishron, skill that succeeds, found only in Ecclesiastes. cheleq (H2506), the portion again: the heir receives as free allotment what cost the builder everything, and natan (H5414), 'leave' is literally 'give' (so the KJV margin).

22.text: For what does a man really have from all his toil, and from the striving of his heart, all that he labors at under the sun?
22.amp: For what has [havah] a man [adam] of all his labour [amal], and of the vexation [raayon -- striving, chasing] of his heart [leb], wherein he has laboured [amel] under the sun?
22.notes: raayon (H7475), the striving or wind-chasing of chapter 1:17, now located inside the chest: the heart itself does the futile herding. havah (H1933), to be or become: what actually accrues to him? The question expects nothing.

23.text: For all his days are pain, and his occupation is grief; even at night his heart cannot lie down and rest. This also is vapor.
23.amp: For all his days [yom] are sorrows [makob -- pains], and his travail [inyan -- task, business] grief [kaas -- vexation]; yea, his heart [leb] takes no rest [shakab -- cannot lie down] in the night [layil]. This is also vapor [hebel].
23.notes: makob (H4341) and kaas (H3708), the same pain-and-vexation pair that closed chapter 1, now describe the workman's whole calendar. shakab (H7901) is to lie down for sleep: the body goes to bed and the heart stays at the desk.

24.text: There is nothing better for a man than to eat and to drink and to let his soul taste good in his toil. This too I saw for what it is: it comes from the hand of God.
24.amp: There is nothing better [tov] for a man [adam], than that he should eat [akal] and drink [shatah], and make his soul [nephesh] see [raah] good [tov] in his labour [amal]. This also I saw [raah], that it was from the hand of God [Elohim].
24.notes: The hinge of the book's first movement. nephesh (H5315) is the whole living self, and 'make his soul see good' (the KJV margin offers 'delight his senses') is receiving the day's bread and work as actual pleasure. The turn is the last clause: such enjoyment cannot be seized, only given, from the hand of Elohim (H430).

25.text: For who can eat, and who can find enjoyment, apart from Him, any more than I could?
25.amp: For who can eat [akal], or who else can hasten [chush -- hurry toward enjoyment] to it, more than I?
25.notes: chush (H2363), to hasten, here of hurrying toward pleasure: if enjoyment could be reached by running, the king with every advantage would have arrived first. His failure proves the gift-character of joy.

26.text: For to the man who is good in His sight God gives wisdom and knowledge and joy; but to the sinner He gives the business of gathering and heaping up, only to hand it over to the one who pleases God. This also is vapor and a chasing after wind.
26.amp: For God [Elohim] gives [natan] to a man [adam] that is good [tov] in His sight [panim -- before His face] wisdom [chokmah], and knowledge [daat], and joy [simchah]: but to the sinner [chet] He gives travail [inyan], to gather [asaph] and to heap up, that He may give to him that is good before God. This also is vapor [hebel] and a chasing after wind [reuth ruach].
26.notes: natan (H5414), to give, three times over: God is the only real distributor in the verse. chet (H2398) is the sinner, whose inyan (H6045), business, is warehouse work for an estate he will never keep (cf. Proverbs 13:22); yet even this ordering, seen only from under the sun, still reads as vapor.
